7 TRIAXIAL STRENGTH (STT) Simplified triaxial compressive strength tests were performed on 1x2 inch vertical samples. The tests were performed on natural moisture samples. The core plug compressive strength was determined by loading axial pressure to the sample in compression bi-axial core holder to sample failure (collapse). The triaxial compressive strength of the sample is defined as the highest pressure reading value before failure. A constant axial hydraulic (hand pump) pressure was applied, at constant radial (2 MPa) confining pressure. The time for hydrostatic loading up to MPa and time for consolidation was minimum minute. The confining pressure was kept constant at MPa and the axial pressure was increased until plug collapse. The time for loading in the shear phase upon rock failure is minimum minutes. The manometer (max. peak memory) read the failure pressure directly in MPa, the only adjustment required was small correction factor for the difference in piston and sample areas. DISCOVERY REPORT WELL 7120/1-2 Suim_p_yar Well 7120/1-2 was spudded on 1st January 1989 as the second and final commitment well in Production Licence 108. The well was planned to test a Lower Cretaceous/Upper Jurassic wedge play immediately to the south of the Loppa High, and drilled to total depth of 2630 in bdf in rocks of Triassic age. The upper of the two seismically-defined wedges was found to comprise silts and shales of Early to Middle Albian age (Wedge In), whilst the lower wedge consisted of two contrasting clastic packages of Valanginian to latest Ryazanian (Wedge IIa) and Early Volgian (Wedge IIb) age respectively. Oil was recovered from RFT's at in (Wedge ha) and in (an isolated sand in the Kimmeridgian Hekkingen Formation). In addition, well-log interpretation revealed low hydrocarbon saturations in sands of the Triassic Fruholmen Formation. Subsequent testing revealed the Fruholmen to be tight and the hydrocarbons to be immovable, but total of 1600 litres light 31°API (0.87 g/cm3 ) oil was recovered from the hydrocarbon-bearing interval in Wedge ha. Evaluation of the test results was hampered by technical problems encountered during the testing. However, RFT pressures together with the petrophysical evaluation suggest single oil column of approximately 90 in in Wedge IIa (Valanginian) with an oil-water contact at about 1970 in bdf. Reservoir parameters in the hydrocarbon-bearing zone are generally poor, with extensive quartz overgrowth and calcite cementation resulting in an average porosity of only 13% and net/gross of 8%. 8 SATURATION 8.1 Dean & Stark Fluid saturation analyses were performed by Dean-Stark method on inch plugs drilled onshore: Plugs for Sw were drilled with Clarisol oil as cooling agent. Water was extracted from the plugs using toluene, giving direct water volume readings. The amount of water extracted from each sample was recorded. Method: Toluene has boiling point of approx. 110°C. When the toluene reaches the boiling point, heat from the toluene vapor causes the water in the sample to evaporate. The toluene- and water vapor both condense in water cooler. The water is collected in water-trap. The toluene in its liquid state flows back and soaks the sample, extracting the oil in the sample. See Figure 8.1, standard D&S equipment setup. The water in the water collector is distilled. Dissolved salts in the formation water are not dissolved by the toluene, and, therefore, remain in the core sample. Subsequent to the Dean&Stark extraction the sample is placed in the soxhlet apparatus using methanol to remove salt deposits in the sample. The extracted water volume is corrected for salt content. correction factor for each depth zone is found using total water volume and total salt weight from all plugs covering each depth zone. Where: w = Distilled water density (g/cm3) b = Brine density (g/cm3) Cs = Dissolved salt concentration (g/l) The salt weight is the plug weight difference prior and after Methanol extraction. Density of brine is based on all salt being NaCl (Sodium Cloride). Complete removal of hydrocarbons was confirmed by visual checking the solvent discoloration, and by examine the sample using UV light. A rig source VSP survey was recorded in this vertical well on 3/10/94. During the survey five runs into the well were required in order to satisfactorily record 170 levels between 970 and 4400m. The source used was Bolt airgun array consisting of four 160 cu.in. guns, positioned 69m from the wellhead along bearing of 70 degrees, and at depth of 4.5m below MSL The source signature was monitored using hydrophone 2m above the array. For the purposes of trial for VSP derived synthetic sonic, data were recorded by dual receiver array positioned at intervals of the same value as the spacing between the two geophones (i.e. 15m). This has meant that there are numerous levels recorded more than once, though this is also due to levels duplicated during the different runs into the well. For the standard processing for this well, generally only the best level data recorded was selected to represent any level shot more than once, although data consistency was also aimed for in deciding which data to use. Note also that no significant timing discrepancies were encountered between such duplicated levels, implying that reasonable depth control was maintained throughout the survey. DATA TIMING AND COMPUTATIONS Noise transmitted through casing sections caused severe problems in timing the majority of the data, particularly for shallowest levels where casing noise arrivals are evident before the expected direct arrivals. In an attempt to identify direct arrivals throughout the bulk of the data, several noise attenuations were carried out. The data was first filtered using restrictive 2,5-40,45 Hz bandpass filter designed to retain most of the signal bandwidth (as seen by F-K analyses) whilst attenuating the casing noise of higher frequencies. Further to this, remaining casing noise has been attenuated through an enhacement and subtraction technique (after coarse downwave subtraction, casing noise was then estimated using a short median operator, this estimate finally being subtracted from the raw data). An automated trace alignment method was used on resultant direct arrival data, improved times generally being obtained as result. However, no usable times could be obtained for the levels at and above 2180m, these levels having to be disregarded due to the contamination from noise transmitted through the casing, nor for the level at 3944m. Final times were therefore obtained for 151 of the levels, although all those seen to be affected by casing noise should still be treated with caution. The check levels have been selected at vertical depth intervals of either 90m (for shallower levels) or 45m (for the deepest levels) in the calculation of interval velocities and for the sectional display of well geophone signals. The Plio-Quaternary Unconformity is seen on seismic data as reflector of laterally variable amplitude. This is to be expected, as the unconformity brings different lithologies in contact with each other and the tuning effects on seismic amplitudes will vary from place to place. In addition, there are some anomalous areas which show indications of gas in the sediments. These indications are: reverse phase top reflector, normal phase basal reflector, highest amplitudes in subtle structural highs, phase reversed lateral truncation, localised edge diffractions, acoustic masking and velocity pull-down of deeper reflectors. The proposed 7122/7-2 well location and the relief well location are both on the edge of an amplitude anomaly at the Plio-Quaternary Unconformity which is likely to be due to gas in the sediments. linear feature, which may be buried iceberg ploughmark with sandy infill, links the western and eastern parts of the anomaly. The thickness of the possible gas bearing interval is estimated to be less than 21 at the proposed 7122/7-2 location and less than 16 at the relief well location. There is no lithology or velocity data from the previous well 7122/7-1 at such shallow level, but realistic velocities would place the top of the possible gas bearing zone at somewhere between 55 and 75 below seabed (432 and 452 MSL). At such shallow level, any gas bearing sandy layer is likely to be normally pressured. The gas may not be moveable. The seismic data do not indicate the gas saturation and moderate to high seismic amplitudes can be produced by only or 10% gas saturation. None the less, due caution should be taken while drilling through the Plio-Quaternary Unconformity. Reference is made to the Askeladden West well 7120/7-1 which had gas bearing sand interval in the Quaternary, from 375 to 392 m. The Base Tertiary Unconformity is of variable seismic amplitude within the site survey area. These lateral changes are interpreted as mostly due to lithological variations and seismic tuning effects. The amplitudes at the proposed 7122/7-2 well location and the relief well location are not anomalously high and the chance of shallow gas at the Base Tertiary Unconformity is assessed as low. The interval in question is less than 10 thick. pilot hole will be drilled through this level and appropriate shallow gas procedures will be followed. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. 4.1 THE CALIBRATION CURVE An example is given in Fig 1. To display the relationship between check level times and integrated sonic log times, cal- ibration curve is produced. This is plot of true vertical depth against the difference be- tween integrated log time and check level time at each check level depth( TVD vs TI-Tc)). The sonic log integrator is time-tied to the corrected time of the shallowest check level in- cluded in the depth range covered by the log. Then the first point on the calibration curve has `Tl-Tc' value of zero. • From the calibration curve, single or series of drift 'shifts' will be indicated by the points implying that the velocities require correction. The points will define both the direction and the magnitude of the shift to be applied to the velocity log. The shifts can be applied from check level to check level but are more often interpolated to change at significant changes of velocity and/or lithology. The danger of not changing drift at significant boundaries is of changing the local character of the log and introducing artificial velocity interfaces. By changing at the ends of lithological units, the reasonable assumption is made that the source of the error is related to lithology.

Fracture systems and breakouts are not directly observable on diplogs (c.f. image logs, such as the CBIL) but valuable information can be obtained from calliper data alone. Boreholes in an anisotropic horizontal stress field tend to become elliptical, with the long axis of the ellipse oriented parallel to the minimum horizontal principle stress. The borehole walls will tend to fail and spall away in this direction, producing vertical grooves known as breakouts (e.g. Hillis & Williams, 1992). The four-arm diplog provides two orthogonal calliper measurements. One calliper will tend to lodge in the long-axis of the borehole ellipse, so that the callipers give an indication of the orientation of borehole elipticity, and hence an insight into the stress field. The borehole in 34/11-1 is only slightly elliptical. Data on borehole eccentricity were obtained by comparing the maximum and minimum calliper values every 0.5m, seeking eccentricities greater than 1.01, ignoring hole sections greater than out of gauge, interpreted as washouts. 1:200 plot of ellipse orientations (in-situ stress analysis) is included in Volume 2. The most obvious feature of these data is strong WNW-ENE preferred orientation (Fig. 11), indicating SSW-NNE orientation for the maximum horizontal principal stress. This orientation is consistent with regional observations on the stress field of the North Viking Graben (Cowgill et al. 1993) but is orthogonal to much of the data for the Tampen Spur (Jorgensen & Bratli, 1995). Open faults/fractures are known to cause local perturbations in the stress field (Bell et al., 1992). Such perturbations provide additional support for fault interpretations from diplogs and some insight into fault orientation. The inferred faults at 4170m and 4040m both show perturbations in the stress field consistent with approximately E-W faulting. Page 18

SPERRY - SUN PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness, drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flowline temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure, i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction, any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) Sonic log: Can be used to calculate pore pressures, using Eaton’s formula, and subsequently confirm and/or revise any pore pressure calculations made whilst drilling. 6608/10-D-1 AH/BH

Drilling Exponent If hole was drilled through good thickness of uniform 'normally' pressured shales, holding parameters of bit size, weight on bit (WOB), rotary speed (RPM) and mud weight constant, gradual reduction in the rate of penetration would be expected, due to the increasingly compacted nature of the sediments encountered and to the increasing differential bottom hole pressure (BHP). If subsequently an overpress- ured zone was encountered, reversal of the 'normal' rate of penetration trend would be seen. This is explained in terms of variation in differential BHP, i.e. if formation pore pressure is greater than bottom hole hydrostatic pressure, then shales will tend to explode into the hole - thus making the overpressured formation comparatively more drillable. In practice, it is not feasible to hold the independent variables of WOB, RPM, bit size and mud weight constant through more than very short section of the hole. Jordan and Shirley (19bb) produced an equation aimed at normalising rate of penetration, with respect to the variables of RPM, WOB, and bit size. The product was known as the 'd' exponent. 'd' = LOG Penetration Rate in Ft/Hr b0 (rev/min) 12 Weight On Bit (lbs) Bit Diameter (ins) 10 A corrected 'd' exponent value related to the mud weight and 'normal' pore pressure, is used to allow for reasonably accurate pore pressure prediction 'dc' normal gradient (ppg) 'd' actual mud weight (ppg) Disadvantages are that not all parameters affecting penetration rate are included in the equation, but these are outweighed by the advantages. GEOLOGICAL HISTORY The deepest sediments encountered in the Statoil 9/2-3 well were claystones and coals attributed to the Bryne Formation (Vestland Group). general Middle Jurassic age is suggested by the long-ranging miospore assemblages present although regionally the Bryne Formation is considered to be of Bajocian to ?Bathonian age. Deltaic/paralic environments of deposition are indicated for this sequence. A stratigraphical hiatus separates the Bryne Formation from the overlying Sandnes Formation (Vestland Group). The Sandnes Formation is predominantly sandstone sequence representing deposition in relatively high energy, shallow marine environment close to terrestrial source. This arenaceous depositional phase is considered to have been initiated by a late Callovian transgression which continued into earliest mid Oxfordian times. Sand deposition was terminated in the Oxfordian and replaced by claystones attributed to the Egersund Formation (Boknfjord Group). These argillaceous sediments represent deposition in relatively nearshore shelf setting and are dated as Oxfordian. An intraformational palynofacies break manifested by reduced terrestrial influences within the late Oxfordian is interpreted as the horizon of the pseudocordata Zone transgressive event. Egersund Formation shelf claystone deposition continued through the early Kimmeridgian into the late Kimmeridgian. A further transgressive event associated with the eudoxus Zone (late Kimmeridgian) was responsible for water mass stratification and the development of anoxic bottom waters which resulted in the deposition of the sapropelic Tau Formation (Boknfjord Group) claystones. Tau Formation sediments are dated as Kimmeridgian to early Volgian in this well. The Tau Formation is conformably overlain by claystones of the Sauda Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as early Volgian to early Ryazanian in age. They are envisaged to have been deposited in generally regressive shelf palaeoenvironment with dysaerobic bottom waters. The Sauda Formation is overlain with apparent conformity by identical claystones of the Flekkefjord Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as late Ryazanian in age. They represent deposition in low energy, ?sub wavebase shelf setting under overall regressive conditions. The Flekkefjord Formation - Valhall Formation (Cromer Knoll Group) boundary which regionally is coincident with the major stenomphalus Zone (intra-late Ryazanian) transgressive event could not be recognised lithologically in this well, although palaeontological and palvnofacies changes were observed. The contact is inferred to equate with the biostratigraphically determined late - latest Ryazanian boundary.

Appendix : Sonic Log Calibration The types of problem which occur with the sonic logs are most commonly either cycle skips, when one receiver fails to detect the true first arrival of the ultrasonic signal, or washouts, where the first arrival has been transmit- ted through the fluid column and not the formation. These types of errors can often be recognised, but cycle skip, in particular, is not obvious if the log has been filtered or is playback. Editing of known errors can remove some of these problems but not all. In the case of washouts, for example, the true formation velocity may not be known accurately. Another problem for the geophysicist is that the velocities measured by the sonic log are often different from seismic velocities, which are obtained by a study of acoustic waves of much greater wavelength. This can be attribut- ed to either the different ways of timing the sonic log waveforms and the seismic check shot arrivals, or to genuine velocity dispersion between the different frequencies. In addition, de-stressing or fluid invasion of the bore- hole wall caused by drilling may alter its acoustic properties. Lastly the sonic log rarely is made up to surface, and thus the velocity in this upper zone is unknown. The absolute travel time to particular depth is therefore not certain. 4.0 CHECK SHOT CALIBRATION Most of these problems can be removed by checkshot calibration. Check- shot calibration is performed in two stages: 1. Tying the log time (TI) with the check shot time (Tc)at specific depth to give an absolute time below datum. This is done using single check shot value. Thus it is fixed that travel time is associated with depth D. 2. Modifying the recorded values so that the integrated travel times from the calibrated log are equal to the interval times from the checkshot levels. Stage is not so simple. It is possible to adjust the log so that all values over given section are changed by few microseconds per foot. This is known as linear shift and is usually applied when the velocities from the sonic log are too high. The assumption made is that the log is in error by constant amount at each reading. An alternative method of modifying log velocities is called differential shift and is usually applied when the log velocities are considered too low. In this case the error is often in low velocity values caused by washouts. To compensate, the low velocities are adjusted more than high velocities. The different types of shifts are discussed in more detail in chapter 4.2. Appendix: Sonic Log Calibration- Page of - Mod. June 30, 1993

In the upper part of the interval soft and sticky light grey clay dominates, only intersected by thick sand lense, consisting of clear to white medium grained quartz grains (from 3 m). From 3037 light brown to redish brown clay occurs, which . is partly silty and slightly calcareous. This clay is interbedded with vary-coloured shales and light grey clay in the lower part of the interval. The shales are light green, light to medium grey and brown to brownish red, firm and fissile and have varying content of silt. Thin limestone streaks (white to light brown) occur through- out the interval. Pyrite, siderite and glauconite occur only in minor amounts.

ABSTRACT Analyses performed on shallow probe and downhole heat flow data from the 1985 Barents Sea survey define the seasonal variation in the shallow (less than 10 meters) thermal regime. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS Good bathymetric maps are of great help in interpreting the outcropping geology between seismic lines. On Figure the previous geological inter- pretation is combined with the new bathymetric map. The steep slope in southwest along the - fault is very striking. On the SW - NE line IKU- 101SK-88, sp 3000-3200, topographic high of about 50 was found and the form was discussed in the Main Report. From the bathymetric map it is clear that the high is not local dome but more the easternmost seen extension of WNW - ESE trending ridge. This trend can also be seen on the three dimensional perspective view (Figure 2.3). The bathymetric map has thus limited the discussion about volcanic intrusions by showing that dome structure probably does not exist. No clear evidence of outcropping volcanic rocks is seen near the drill site. In combination with the seismic evidence of possible subcropping volcanic rocks (e. g. the strong disturbance and loss of reflection continuity on line IKU-0822SK-88, sp 2700-2900) there might be subcropping dike system in the area as indicated on Figure 4.1. From the shallow drilling program in 1989 it seems probable that also the Paleozoic rocks found outcropping east of 9°E in the Skagerrak area is of mainly Cambro-Silurian age. Core 13/2-U-2 was postmature, but evaluating the above suggested existence of volcanic dike, we still find it very probable that this was caused by later Paleozoic intrusions. This is also supported by the supposed migrated hydrocarbon content in the core. We therefore find it highly valuable to continue the investigation of the Paleozoic rocks in the Skagerrak area. Our recommendation is to acquire shallow seismic data between 9° and 10° and then continue with shallow drilling based on the results of the seismic.

This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The stratigraphic succession observed in 34/11-2S is complicated by repeated faulting of Brent Group and Viking Group, Heather Formation sediments. Details of these fault repeats are discussed in the biostratigraphy and lithostratigraphy chapters of this report. The oldest sediments analysed are very fine to coarse grained sandstones of the Statfjord Formation which accumulated in fluvial to marine, inner shelf environment during Sinemurian?-Early Pliensbachian times. Following marine transgression during Sinemurian?-Early Pliensbachian to Late Pliensbachian times, deposition of the Dunlin Group, Amundsen and Burton Formation occurred in marine, inner shelf conditions. Sands of the Cook Formation accumulated in marine, inner shelf environment during Late Pliensbachian and Early Toarcian times. These sands were succeeded during Early Toarcian to Late Toarcian times by the Drake Formation. A regional regressive event at the end of beginning of Aalenian times led to the development of fluviodeltaic-marginal marine conditions and the accumulation of the Brent Group. Initial deposition of the Broom Formation took place during Aalenian times. During Aalenian?- Early Bajocian times continued deposition of the Rannoch Formation was succeeded by the Etive Formation and more argillaceous deposits of the Ness Formation. The Ness Formation and Tarbert Formation were deposited during Aalenian?-Early Bajocian, Bajocian and Bajocian-?Bathonian and Early Bathonian times. The Early Bathonian, Middle? Bathonian and Late? Bathonian sediments of the Viking Group, Heather Formation sensu stricto accumulated during transgressive phase in marine, inner shelf setting with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. Deposition of claystones continued through to early Callovian times in similar environmental setting. Deposition was interrupted, possibly because of regional regressive phase, resulting in the absence of middle and late Callovian aged sediments. Heather Formation deposition continued during Early Oxfordian times and was followed by period of erosion or non deposition. Following renewed subsidence, the Late Jurassic transgressive phase resumed during Kimmeridgian?-?Ryazanian times with the accumulation of claystones of the Draupne Formation in mid to outer shelf environment with dysaerobic to anaerobic sea floor conditions. The oldest Cromer Knoll Group sediments consist of calcareous claystones of Early? Albian age and are succeeded, following short period of erosion or non deposition, by Late Albian sediments. The transgressive phase continued into Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian times when claystones of the Shetland Group were deposited in marine outer shelf to upper bathyal environment. High sedimentation and subsidence rates throughout the Late Cretaceous resulted in the accumulation of complete Shetland Group sequence of Cenomanian age through to Late Maastrichtian age. GEOLOGICAL COMPLETION REPORT 6404/11-1 SUMMARY GENERAL PL 254 was awarded to consortium comprising BP Amoco, TotalFinaElf, Norske Conoco and the SDFI (now Petoro AS) as part of the 16th Licencing Round on the 20th May 2000. BP Amoco operate the licence. The pre-drill objective of well 6404/11-1 was to test three primary reservoir targets at T50, K90 and K80 levels and have an option to test one secondary target at K72 level in the Havsule Prospect. The prospect is seismically defined north - south trending structural dome located in the north of the Møre Basin in the Norwegian Sea that is thought to have developed during the Tertiary Period in response to compression during opening of the North Atlantic Ocean. OPERATIONS BP Amoco took over the dynamically positioned (DP) semi-submersible rig, Scarabeo 5, at 19:00 hrs on 14th November 2001 with the rig arriving at the Havsule location at 15:00 hrs on the 24th November 2001. DP trials were undertaken and after the seafloor transponders were deployed, the 6404/11-1 well was spudded at 21:30 hrs on the 1st December 2001. A 12 1/4” pilot hole was drilled from seabed to 2195 mBRT in one bit run. No indications of shallow gas or abnormal pore pressures were observed from drilling data or on LWD. After drilling to section TD the bit was pulled and the hole opened to 36” to 1629 mBRT. While repositioning one of the subsea marker buoys it was inadvertently dropped into the hole necessitating re-spud of the well 28.6m to the north-north west of the original hole location. The well was re-spudded at 13:30 hrs on the 6th December 2001 using 42” 36” hole opener assembly. 26” hole was drilled to 2175 mBRT with seawater and hi-vis sweeps. After displacing to seawater, circulating the hole clean and pulling to 1870 mBRT bubbles were seen flowing from the wellhead. Drillpipe was run to bottom and the hole was made static with 1.20sg mud. Casing was run and cemented without problem, however weather delayed running the BOP’s and riser. The 17” hole section was TD’d 15m shallow to prognosis due to concerns over increasing pore pressure. After running and cementing the 13 3/8” casing it was necessary to run piggy-back casing hanger to allow the seal assembly to seat in the correct position. A value of 1.38sg was obtained for the leak-off after drilling out the 13 3/8” casing and drilling 12 1/4” hole commenced. Drilling was halted at 2730 mBRT when pore pressure was seen to have reached 1.25sg and the bit was pulled into the casing shoe. In an attempt to carry on drilling an open-hole leak-off was performed that confirmed the 1.38sg value obtained earlier. Having insufficient kick tolerance to drill ahead, the decision was made to run 5/8” liner. triple-combo wireline log was run to acquire data over the drilled section. Liner was set and 1.47sg leak-off was obtained. Drilling commenced in 1/2” hole. No reservoir horizons were identified and the well was TD’d at 02:45 hrs on the 20th February at depth of 3650 mBRT. Three wireline logging runs were performed. The 6404/11-1 well was plugged and abandoned as dry hole at 22:00 hrs on the 10th March 2002 and the rig released to Norsk Hydro. Upper Cretaceous (K90 sandstones) were absent and K80 (Nise Formation) sandstones were poorly developed. The well was not extended to penetrate the deeper, K72 (Lysing Formation) secondary target.

4.2 DRILL STEM TESTS Two drill stem tests were carried out, one in the oil zones of each of the Brent Group and Sognefjord Formations. DST flowed oil and free gas from the Brent Group. DST flowed oil from the Sognefjord Formation. Bottom-hole sampling was carried out in DST and DST 2. Two samples were recovered from the Brent Group in DST 1, and samples were recovered from the Sognefjord formation in DST 2, for direct PVT analysis. Surface sampling was carried out in both DST's to obtain samples for recombination and PVT analysis. 4.2.1 Methodology for Interpretation The DST interpretations were carried out using the SAPHER PC interpretation package. All interpretations used the superposition method. The methodology used was: 1. Create Derivative/Log-Log plot to carry out diagnostics of the test, identify flow regions (early, middle and late time regions) and identify the reservoir and boundary models to be used in the analysis. This plot was used to identify the infinite-acting flow region and plot correct Homer straight line on the Semilog or Superposition plot. 2. Plot infinite-acting straight line on Superposition plot and identify main reservoir characteristics (permeability-thickness, skin). 3. Perform any supplementary plots that may assist in identifying character of late time flow (i.e., square-root of time plot for linear flow). 4. Return to Derivative/Log-Log plot and perform time and pressure match to dimensionless functions. Identify reservoir and boundary models to be used and generate synthetic dimensionless derivative and log-log functions for the model. Compare these with the test data. Iterate until good match is obtained. 5. Use the simulation capability to generate the synthetic pressure function from the final chosen model and the calculated reservoir parameters. Compare the synthetic pressure with the test pressure data to ensure that good match is obtained over the whole test, not just the portion being analyzed.

The remainder of the well section, from the hot shale of the Upper Jurassic Mandal Formation to T.D. at 4458 mBRT, was in contrast quite different from forecast. This effort was successful only in part, owing to the absence of diagnostic microfossils over critical intervals of the drilled section. It was thus necessary to terminate the well without the support of age determinations to testify that Top Triassic had been reached. Subsequently, the Stratigraphy Branch of BP Sunbury undertook follow-up study on sidewall core material, their final results being presented in report by Lowe et al. (1983). The interval 4050-4109 mBRT yielded dinoflagellate cysts of Early Portlandian to Late Kimmeridgian age. Among the species reported were Glossodinium dimorphum with latest appearance at 4050 mBRT.
